about: The scripted AI lesson for p3-changes-of-state (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p3-particle-model and p1-heating.

keyPoints.heading: Temperature during changes of state — the heating curve

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about the temperature of something while it melts or boils, and how much energy it takes to change it from one state (solid, liquid or gas) to another.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. Ice is melting. Which is true of its temperature while it melts?
steps.right: Yes: it stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.

wrong.other: Not quite: it stays the same until all the ice has melted.
wrong.rises: Not quite: while ice melts, its temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.
wrong.falls: Not quite: energy is going in, and the temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.

idk.hint: Think of a glass of water with ice in it. Does it warm up while there is still ice in it?

steps.answerWhy: While ice melts, its temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.

steps.question: Second: what is the specific heat capacity of a substance?

options.text: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of it by 1 °C
The energy needed to melt 1 kg of it
The temperature at which it boils

steps.right: Yes: the energy to warm 1 kg of it by 1 °C.

wrong.other: Not quite: it is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C.
wrong.melt: Not quite: that is a different quantity, coming up in this lesson. Specific heat capacity is the energy to warm 1 kg by 1 °C.
wrong.boil: Not quite: that is the boiling point. Specific heat capacity is the energy to warm 1 kg by 1 °C.

idk.hint: Specific heat capacity is the c in ΔE = m c Δθ, where Δθ is a change in temperature. Which button is about changing a temperature?

steps.answerWhy: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Put a thermometer in ice from a freezer and heat it steadily. A graph of its temperature against time is called a heating curve.
At first the line climbs as the ice warms up. At 0 °C the line goes flat: this is the ice melting.
Next the water warms up, so the line climbs again. At 100 °C it goes flat while the water boils. Once all the water has boiled, the steam warms up.
Temperature goes with the particles' kinetic energy, their energy of movement: faster particles mean a higher temperature.
Energy goes in all the time, even on the flat parts.
On a flat part the energy overcomes forces between the particles, raising their potential energy: the energy stored by those forces.
The particles' kinetic energy does not change, so neither does the temperature.
The energy that changes the state, without changing the temperature, is called latent heat. Latent means hidden: the thermometer does not show it.

steps.question: On a heating curve for water, what is going on during the flat part at 100 °C?

options.text: The water has stopped taking in energy

steps.right: Yes: the water is boiling, so the temperature stays at 100 °C.

wrong.other: Not quite: the water is boiling.
wrong.warm: Not quite: warming up makes the line climb. A flat part at 100 °C means the water is boiling.
wrong.stopped: Not quite: energy is still going in. On the flat part it pulls the particles apart as the water boils.

steps.answerWhy: A flat part is a change of state: at 100 °C the water is boiling.

steps.question: On the sloping parts of a heating curve, which energy of the particles is rising?
steps.right: Yes: the particles move faster, so their kinetic energy rises and the temperature goes up.

wrong.pot: Not quite: potential energy rises on the flat parts. On the sloping parts the temperature rises, so the particles' kinetic energy rises.
wrong.none: Not quite: the temperature is rising, so the particles are moving faster: their kinetic energy rises.

idk.hint: On a sloping part the temperature goes up. Which energy is linked to temperature?

steps.answerWhy: On a sloping part the temperature rises, so the particles' kinetic energy rises.

steps.text: Cooling gives the opposite graph, called a cooling curve. The line falls, then goes flat during each change of state, because the substance gives out latent heat as its particles pull back together.

steps.question: Liquid wax cools in a test tube. Its temperature falls, stays at 55 °C for 5 minutes, then falls again. What is going on at 55 °C?
steps.right: Yes: the wax is freezing, giving out latent heat, so its temperature stays at 55 °C.

wrong.other: Not quite: the wax is freezing.
wrong.boil: Not quite: boiling needs energy in, and the wax is cooling. A flat part while cooling means the liquid wax is freezing.
wrong.melt: Not quite: melting needs energy in, and the wax is cooling. A flat part while a liquid cools means it is freezing.

idk.hint: The wax is cooling down. Which change of state happens to a liquid as it cools?

steps.answerWhy: A flat part on a cooling curve is a change of state: the liquid wax is freezing, giving out latent heat.

steps.prompt: In one line: why is part of a heating curve flat?
points: the energy raises the particles' potential energy, not their kinetic energy, so the temperature stays the same
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: on a flat part the substance is changing state; the energy raises the particles' potential energy, so the temperature stays the same.

keyPoints.heading: Specific latent heat — the equation E = mL

steps.text: Different substances need different amounts of energy to change state. The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance, with no change in temperature, is its specific latent heat.
The energy to melt 1 kg, or given out when 1 kg freezes, is the specific latent heat of fusion: here fusion means melting. For water it is 334 000 J/kg: joules for every kilogram.

The energy to boil 1 kg, or given out when 1 kg of gas condenses back to liquid, is the specific latent heat of vaporisation: the energy per kilogram to boil or condense a substance. For water it is 2 260 000 J/kg, almost seven times as much.

steps.question: Predict: which takes more energy, melting 1 kg of ice or boiling away 1 kg of water?
steps.right: Yes: far more for boiling. Next, why.

wrong.other: Not quite: boiling away the water. Next, why.
wrong.melt: Not quite: boiling takes far more, almost seven times as much. Next, why.
wrong.same: Not quite: boiling takes far more, almost seven times as much. Next, why.

idk.hint: Compare the two values for water: 334 000 J/kg to melt, 2 260 000 J/kg to boil. Which is bigger?

steps.answerWhy: Boiling 1 kg of water takes 2 260 000 J, far more than the 334 000 J to melt 1 kg of ice.

steps.text: Vaporisation needs more because boiling must pull the particles completely apart, far from each other. Melting only loosens them: they stay close together.

The equation is E = mL: energy = mass × specific latent heat. E is the energy in joules (J), m is the mass that changes state in kilograms (kg), and L is the specific latent heat in joules per kilogram (J/kg).
Do not mix up the two "specific" quantities. Latent heat is for a change of state at a steady temperature; heat capacity is for a change of temperature within one state.

steps.question: A kettle keeps 1 kg of water boiling at 100 °C until it has all gone. Which value tells you the energy needed?

options.text: The specific latent heat of vaporisation
The specific latent heat of fusion

steps.right: Yes: the water changes from liquid to gas, so it is the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

wrong.other: Not quite: the specific latent heat of vaporisation.
wrong.shc: Not quite: the temperature stays at 100 °C, so this is not specific heat capacity. Liquid to gas uses the specific latent heat of vaporisation.
wrong.fusion: Not quite: fusion is melting. Liquid to gas uses the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

idk.hint: The temperature stays at 100 °C while the water turns into a gas. Which value is about changing from liquid to gas?

steps.answerWhy: The state changes from liquid to gas with no temperature change, so it is the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the specific latent heat of fusion?
points: the energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance, with no change in its temperature.

steps.text: Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: How much energy is needed to melt 2 kg of ice at 0 °C? L for melting ice is 334 000 J/kg.
Your turn. How much energy is needed to boil away 0.5 kg of water at 100 °C? L for boiling water is 2 260 000 J/kg. Give the energy in joules.

wrong.divide: Not quite: 1 130 000 J. Multiply the mass by L, do not divide: 0.5 × 2 260 000 = 1 130 000 J.

idk.hint: Use E = mL: multiply the mass, 0.5, by L, 2 260 000.

steps.text: Masses are often given in grams: change them into kilograms first, by dividing by 1000. For example, 250 g is 0.25 kg.
Here is a worked example of finding L. Its steps open one at a time.
steps.question: 500 g of a solid takes in 150 000 J as it melts at a steady temperature. What is its specific latent heat?
steps: Change the mass into kilograms: 500 g = 0.5 kg.
Put the numbers into E = mL: 150 000 = 0.5 × L.
Divide both sides by 0.5: L = 150 000 ÷ 0.5 = 300 000 J/kg.

steps.question: 200 g of ice melts. L for melting ice is 334 000 J/kg. How much energy did it take in, in joules?

wrong.grams: Not quite: 66 800 J. Change grams into kilograms first: 200 g = 0.2 kg. Then E = 0.2 × 334 000 = 66 800 J.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 66 800 J. Change 200 g into 0.2 kg, then multiply: E = 0.2 × 334 000 = 66 800 J.

idk.hint: First change 200 g into kilograms by dividing by 1000. Then multiply by 334 000.

steps.text: Sometimes you are given a mass before and a mass after. The m in E = mL is only the mass that changed state: the difference between the two.

steps.question: A beaker of water has a mass of 0.250 kg. After boiling for a while it has a mass of 0.240 kg. A joulemeter, which measures the energy supplied, shows 23 000 J. What is L, in J/kg?
steps.right: Yes: 2 300 000 J/kg. The mass boiled away is 0.010 kg, so L = 23 000 ÷ 0.010. Real experiments are never exact, so it is close to, not equal to, 2 260 000 J/kg.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2 300 000 J/kg. The mass that boiled is 0.010 kg, so L = 23 000 ÷ 0.010 = 2 300 000 J/kg.
wrong.whole: Not quite: only the water that boiled away changed state: 0.250 − 0.240 = 0.010 kg. L = 23 000 ÷ 0.010 = 2 300 000 J/kg.
wrong.after: Not quite: use the mass that boiled away, 0.250 − 0.240 = 0.010 kg. L = 23 000 ÷ 0.010 = 2 300 000 J/kg.

idk.hint: First find the mass that boiled away: 0.250 − 0.240. Then put the numbers into E = mL and divide both sides by that mass.

steps.answerWhy: The mass boiled away is 0.010 kg, so L = E ÷ m = 23 000 ÷ 0.010 = 2 300 000 J/kg.

steps.question: To measure L for melting ice in the lab, which two things must you measure?

options.text: The energy supplied and the mass of ice melted
The mass of the funnel and the heater

steps.right: Yes: E and m, the two quantities in E = mL.

wrong.other: Not quite: the energy supplied and the mass of ice melted.
wrong.temp: Not quite: the temperature does not change while ice melts. You need E and m: the energy supplied and the mass of ice melted.
wrong.funnel: Not quite: the funnel and heater do not melt. You need E and m: the energy supplied and the mass of ice melted.

idk.hint: Look at E = mL. Which two quantities can you measure, to work out L?

steps.answerWhy: E = mL, so you measure the energy supplied, E, and the mass of ice melted, m.

steps.text: To measure L for melting ice, put crushed ice in a funnel with an electric heater in it, connected to a joulemeter. The melted water drips into a beaker, and its mass is found on a balance.
The warm room melts some ice too. To allow for that, set up a second funnel of ice with no heater on, and take its melted mass away from the first.
From the measurements, L = E ÷ m, where m is the mass melted by the heater alone, after taking away the room's share.

steps.question: In this practical, some energy from the heater warms the air instead of the ice. Is the value of L you calculate too high or too low?
steps.right: Yes: the joulemeter counts all the energy, but less ice melts, so E ÷ m comes out too big.

wrong.low: Not quite: the joulemeter still counts all the energy, but less ice melts. A big E over a small m gives an L that is too high.
wrong.same: Not quite: the energy lost still shows on the joulemeter, but melts no ice. So E ÷ m comes out too high.

idk.hint: All the energy is counted in E, but less ice melts, so m is smaller. Does a smaller m make E ÷ m bigger or smaller?

steps.answerWhy: All the energy is counted but less ice melts, so E ÷ m comes out too high.

steps.prompt: In one line: in E = mL, what is m, and what unit must it be in?
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: m is the mass that changes state, in kilograms.

steps.text: Evaporation is a liquid turning into a gas at its surface, at any temperature, far below its boiling point. Like boiling, it takes in latent heat.
Sweat is mostly water. As it evaporates from your skin it takes in over 2 000 000 J for every kilogram. That energy comes from your body, so you cool down.
Sweating cools you best in hot, dry air. In humid air, which already holds a lot of water vapour, sweat evaporates slowly, so you cool down less.

steps.question: Steam at 100 °C burns skin far worse than water at 100 °C. Predict why.

options.text: As it condenses on the skin, it gives out latent heat as well

steps.right: Yes: condensing gives out latent heat. Next, the details.

wrong.other: Not quite: as it condenses on the skin, it gives out latent heat as well. Next, the details.
wrong.hotter: Not quite: here both are at 100 °C. The difference is that steam condenses on the skin. Next, the details.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: particles are the same size in every state. The difference is that steam condenses on the skin. Next, the details.

idk.hint: Steam turns into water on the skin. Does a gas give out or take in latent heat when it condenses?

steps.answerWhy: Steam gives out latent heat as it condenses on the skin, on top of the energy the hot water gives out as it cools.

steps.text: When steam touches skin it condenses, giving out its latent heat of vaporisation to the skin: 2 260 000 J for every kilogram.
Once the steam has condensed, the hot water on the skin cools and gives out more energy. Water at 100 °C gives out only the energy it releases as it cools.

steps.prompt: In one line: how does sweating cool you down?
points: it takes energy (latent heat) from your body
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: sweat evaporates, taking latent heat from your skin, so your body cools.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: a flat part on a heating curve shows…?
steps.right: Yes: a change of state, at a steady temperature.

wrong.other: Not quite: a change of state.
wrong.w1: Not quite: warming up makes the line climb. A flat part is a change of state.
wrong.w2: Not quite: energy is still going in. A flat part is a change of state.

steps.answerWhy: A flat part on a heating curve is a change of state at a steady temperature.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: how much energy melts 3 kg of ice? L = 334 000 J/kg. Give it in joules.
Quiz, question 3 of 6: how much energy boils away 100 g of water? L = 2 260 000 J/kg. Give it in joules.
Quiz, question 4 of 6: a substance takes in 90 000 J to melt 0.3 kg. What is its L, in J/kg?
Quiz, question 5 of 6: which is the specific latent heat of fusion?

options.text: The energy to melt 1 kg with no change in temperature
The energy to boil 1 kg with no change in temperature
The energy to warm 1 kg by 1 °C

wrong.other: Not quite: the energy to melt 1 kg with no change in temperature.
wrong.w1: Not quite: boiling uses the specific latent heat of vaporisation. Fusion means melting.
wrong.w2: Not quite: that is specific heat capacity. Fusion means melting: the energy to melt 1 kg.

steps.answerWhy: The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy to melt 1 kg with no change in temperature.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: which of these gives out latent heat?
steps.right: Yes: condensing gives out latent heat as the particles pull back together.

wrong.w1: Not quite: melting takes latent heat in. Condensing gives it out.
wrong.w2: Not quite: boiling takes latent heat in. Condensing gives it out.

steps.answerWhy: Condensing and freezing give out latent heat; melting and boiling take it in.
